# A uniform slab-tail bound for centered concave sequences

Let `(w_i)` be a nonzero, nonnegative concave sequence on a finite interval
of consecutive integers. Suppose `sum_i i w_i=0`. Set

    M=sum_i w_i,   Q=sum_i w_i^2,   m=max_i w_i.

Terms outside its index interval are defined to be zero for sums, without
asserting concavity across the artificial endpoints. For every integer
`h>=0`, both tails satisfy

    sum_(i>h) w_i >= [M-(2h+1)m]/3,
    sum_(i<-h) w_i >= [M-(2h+1)m]/3.                  (1)

This is a scalar theorem. Its proof below does not use a mixed-integer
centerpoint or Grunbaum assertion. Zero endpoint terms may be removed:
positive terms form an interval, the mass and mean do not change, and
concavity is retained. Write its positive support as `[l,r]` and its
cardinality as N. All subsequent square roots concern actual positive tails.

## 1. The two elementary sequence estimates needed

First,

    Q>(2/3)mM,   and consequently w_0>=Q/M>(2/3)m.     (2)

Here is a short proof of the strict quadratic estimate. For a concave
sequence `x_0,...,x_s` anchored at `x_0=1`, the quadratic expression
`sum(x_i^2-2x_i/3)` has minimum `(s+1)/(3(2s+1))` at
`v_i=1-2i/(2s+1)`. To verify it, for s>=1 put e=x-v and
`G_t(i)=min(i,t)-it/s`. Then

    e_i=(i/s)e_s+sum_(t=1)^(s-1) a_t G_t(i),
    a_t=2e_t-e_(t-1)-e_(t+1)>=0.

For `b_i=v_i-1/3`, direct sums give

    sum b_i i=0,
    sum b_i G_t(i)=t(s-t)(s+1-t)/(3(2s+1))>=0.

Expanding the quadratic difference yields `sum e_i^2+2sum b_i e_i>=0`.
The case s=0 is direct. Apply this result on both sides of a maximum
index j of w/m, subtracting the duplicated peak contribution 1/3. It gives

    Q-(2/3)mM >= (m^2/6)[1/(2(j-l)+1)+1/(2(r-j)+1)]>0.

The weighted Jensen inequality for the piecewise affine concave interpolation
of w, with weights w_i/M and mean zero, gives `w_0>=Q/M`. A singleton is
included; otherwise the zero mean places index zero strictly between the
positive extremes. This proves (2).

Second, when N>=4,

    m/M<=1/2.                                        (3)

For N>=5, concavity puts each side of the maximum above the chord from
the maximum to zero at its corresponding endpoint. If both sides have
positive length, summing those chords gives `M>=m(N-1)/2>=2m`. If the
maximum is an endpoint, the one full chord gives `M>=mN/2`, which is
stronger. For N=4, the integer mean is one of the two internal indices.
After reflection the indices are -1,0,1,2 and the widths are a,b,c,e.
The zero mean and concavity give

    a=c+2e,   c+e<=b<=2c-e,
    M=b+2c+3e.

These relations imply separately `2a<=M`, `2b<=M`, `2c<=M`, and `2e<=M`.
This proves (3), including nonsymmetric supports.

## 2. Square roots of actual suffix sums are concave

Set `F_j=sum_(i=j)^r w_i` for l<=j<=r. Then `sqrt(F_j)` is a concave
sequence on THESE indices. In particular, its decrements

    delta_j=sqrt(F_j)-sqrt(F_(j+1)),   l<=j<r,

are nondecreasing. No decrement from r to an artificial zero is included.

For a proof at an internal index j, put F=F_j, a=w_(j-1), b=w_j.
If a<=b, then `F_(j-1)+F_(j+1)<=2F`, and square-root concavity suffices.
Otherwise put D=a-b>0. Positivity of w_(j+1) and concavity imply b>D.
For all available k>=0, `w_(j+k)<=b-kD`, so

    F<=D sum_(k>=0)(q-k)_+,   q=b/D>1.

Writing theta for the fractional part of q, the arithmetic sum is

    sum_(k>=0)(q-k)_+
      =(q^2+q+theta(1-theta))/2 <=(2q+1)^2/8.

Thus `F<=(a+b)^2/[8(a-b)]`. Since F>=b>D/2, squaring twice, with both
right sides nonnegative, shows that this is exactly the condition

    sqrt(F+a)+sqrt(F-b)<=2sqrt(F).

This proves every required midpoint inequality.

## 3. A discrete packing estimate

If a nonnegative sequence of mass A is supported on integers at most h
and all its entries are at most m, then its first moment is at most

    hA-A^2/(2m)+A/2.                                 (4)

Indeed, write A=q m+s with q a nonnegative integer and 0<=s<m. Filling
the nearest indices h,h-1,... maximizes the first moment. Its value is
`hA-mq(q-1)/2-qs`. The difference between the lower bound
`mq(q-1)/2+qs` for the distance moment and `A^2/(2m)-A/2` is
`s(m-s)/(2m)>=0`. This proves (4) without a continuous replacement.

## 4. Proof of the right-tail bound

It suffices to treat a proposed failure of (1). Put k=2h+1 and
`T=sum_(i>h)w_i`. Such a failure requires

    0<=T<(M-km)/3<=M/3.                              (5)

If T=0, apply (4) to the whole sequence. Its zero first moment implies
`0<=hM-M^2/(2m)+M/2`, or M<=km, contrary to (5). Hence T>0.

First assume N>=4. We claim that the right-tail distance moment satisfies

    E:=sum_(i>h)(i-h)w_i
       <=T+2sqrt(M) T^(3/2)/(3m).                    (6)

If there is only one right-tail term, E=T, so (6) is immediate.
Otherwise put s=h+1<r and c=m/(2sqrt(M)). Choose an index p with w_p=m.
If p<=s, it is strictly below r, and Section 2 gives

    delta_s>=delta_p
      =m/(sqrt(F_p)+sqrt(F_(p+1)))>=c.

If p>s, concavity between indices 0 and p gives w_s>=w_0>2m/3. Since
F_s=T, equations (2) and (5) give

    delta_s=w_s/(sqrt(T)+sqrt(F_(s+1)))
       >m/(3sqrt(T))>m/(2sqrt(M))=c.

All subsequent actual decrements are at least c. Consequently, for every
integer v>=0,

    F_(s+v) <= (sqrt(T)-v c)_+^2,                    (7)

where F is set to zero beyond r only for this estimate. For s+v<=r the
bound follows by adding actual decrements; its right side must then be
positive. For s+v>r its left side is zero, so no extra concavity assumption
is needed. Finally, finite summation by parts and the decreasing nonnegative
function in (7) give

    E=sum_(v>=0) F_(s+v)
      <=T+integral_0^infinity (sqrt(T)-xc)_+^2 dx
      =T+T^(3/2)/(3c).

This is (6).

Apply (4) to the mass A=M-T at indices at most h and use (6) on the other
side. The zero first moment implies

    0 <= hM-(M-T)^2/(2m)+(M-T)/2
                      +T+2sqrt(M)T^(3/2)/(3m).

With t=T/M and mu=m/M, rearrange this as

    (h+1/2)mu
      >=(1-t)^2/2-(2/3)t^(3/2)-mu t/2.              (8)

The right side of (8), minus `1/2-3t/2`, equals

    t[1/2+t/2-(2/3)sqrt(t)-mu/2].

For t>=0,

    1/2+t/2-(2/3)sqrt(t)
       =5/18+(sqrt(t)-2/3)^2/2>=5/18.

By (3), mu<=1/2, so this difference is at least t/36>0. Therefore
`k mu>1-3t`, contradicting (5). This proves the bound for N>=4.

For N=3, the integer zero mean places the indices at -1,0,1, with widths
a,b,a and b>=a. Thus m=b and the right tail at h=0 is
`a=(M-m)/2>=(M-m)/3`; for h>=1 its claimed right side is nonpositive.
For N=1 the sole positive index is zero and the assertion is immediate.
There is no positive two-term sequence on consecutive integers with an
integer mean. These observations cover all remaining cases.

Reflection of indices proves the left-tail bound. Every bound above is
finite and exact. Neither an artificial terminal concavity node nor a
limiting sequence is used.
